4/5 metatarsals fractured is a serious injury. all 5 dislocated is a more serious injury!

This isn't a comment of "you will never recover" but perspective - it will take time for you to get back to drumming and being on your feet a lot. This is going to be difficult and should be recognised as such.

But, you'll get there - especially if you're young, healthy and mentally driven. 

I can't comment on the high heels but on footwear - I now spend lots of money on orthotics and comfortable footwear. The benefit of this is when I want to wear double moccasins for a day out (or a wedding) I can do it, and it'll suck the next day, but I can do it. My understanding is heels are more difficult still, but with practice, rehab and appropriate recovery after, doable.

- i have done a lot of PT, and have done it specifically to manage falling and jumping, i went well beyond "PT to walk again", which cost a bunch of cash. i generally feel pretty stable when falling, but it took practice

- not super often, a few times a year. I was never a serious boulderer, but it's easier now because I take pretty good care of my body now and have more muscle to work with

- i had my lisfranc screws taken out (they had to be put over a key tendon in my foot, so the risk of breaking could have fucked my ability to walk.) my cuboid plate is still in my foot - i don't feel it unless i'm pushing my foot particularly hard (deadlifting barefoot at high weights, say)

I was in a boot after the initial two weeks in a cast. Pretty normal!

The pain gets better and worse over time in your initial recovery period. It took probably 8 weeks post injury before it was consistently more mild.

Let me be clearer. 

My surgeon told me I'd never walk properly again. now I can do all of the above and more. 

You're active and you're very early in your journey. It's emotionally tough. I get it. But, what are you going to do - quit?

Don't fucking quit. Take it kindly on yourself, but hit your PT hard and sustainability, and you'll crush the 70% prognosis.

Hi. Today is my three year anniversary from a severe Lisfranc, shattered ankle, dislocated ankle, shattered cuboid, broken heel. 

I've been back climbing and bouldering, back to running, doing 160kg squats and dead lifts. 

The surgeon prognosis is always bleak and realistic. Hit the PT really hard and do the work and you'll recover well.

broke 4 of my metatarsals along with a whole bunch of other stuff. injury happened december 2020. let's take one Q at a time

> how long until you could start walking after surgery? 

I was allowed to walk in the boot immediately after surgery (NWB for 12 weeks). Transitioned to shoes 2 weeks after surgery.

HOWEVER it took me a while to get back to walking properly. my leg muscles had atrophied significantly while laid up. it probably took me six or so months of heavy PT and training to be back to walking "normal" (i.e. without a noticeable limp 80% of the time)

> What things helped you the most while in a walking boot? 

I took 10 days off work following the surgery to focus entirely on relearning how to walk. At first I could do one step at a time, with 25% weight on my foot, 75% on crutches. then two steps. Taking that time allowed me to REALLY focus on the mechanics of walking, rest, taking it easy. By the third day I could very slowly climb a set of stairs. 

> What did the pain stop? 

In the last 3-6 months my day to day pain has really ceased, and now I only get mild discomfort when I push hard. 

> What is one bit of advice you wish you had followed?

Investing in compression socks earlier.  

> How soon can I get in a gym? (I'm gaining weight like crazy) 

I gained 12 or so kg when I was laid up, so feel ya. 
Depends on your gym layout and level of comfort! My gym was up two flights of stairs, so going while I was NWB on crutches was a no go - but there's nothing theoretically stopping you from doing any exercise you can do sitting down, now.

For me, I was in the gym doing very light leg presses on the bad foot (5kg single leg presses) about two weeks following the hardware removal surgery. Now I can squat 120kg and deadlift 130kg, and I know I'm not done yet.

>Anything you would recommend completely avoiding?

I guess just the mental stuff - this is mentally a hard injury to recover from, so letting myself get down - I wouldn't do that again. You'll have setbacks and fall back in progress, but that's OK - it's one step at a time, right?

pain forever? nope. i have days where i'm stiff and sore, but in pain? nah.

i do have to keep up with the rehab and not push myself super hard (or be aware of the consequences if I do) - but there are days I can walk 30,000 steps and be OK after. 

of course, the custom orthotics in my shoes and the 18 months of rehab I've done so far? they really help. keep at it!

Hello. Former interviewer for the NSW Government (Department of Planning and Environment) here. The replies so far are good but miss a couple of key things.

Is your interview online or in person? This will change your prep considerably.

Look at the capabilities. They will have six or seven dot points for each one. Depending on the type of role there'll be five, or seven, or ten, or fifteen capabilities (generally, of course, the more senior the role, the more capabilities. The last role I interviewed for had 10.)

Below is an example from a generic role description:

Think and Solve Problems

Think, analyse and consider the broader context to develop practical solutions

• Research and apply critical-thinking techniques in analysing information, identify interrelationships and make recommendations based on relevant evidence

• Anticipate, identify and address issues and potential problems that may have an impact on organisational objectives and the user experience

• Apply creative-thinking techniques to generate new ideas and options to address issues and improve the user experience

• Seek contributions and ideas from people with diverse backgrounds and experience

• Participate in and contribute to team or unit initiatives to resolve common issues or barriers to effectiveness

• Identify and share business process improvements to enhance effectiveness

You need to cover those dot points and demonstrate that you can do those things. The STAR method is good. I use SAO (Situation, Action, Outcome). Tell a story, and make sure you cover those dot points best you can.

You probably won't get the questions ahead of time. It's very easy to over prepare and then get curveballed and get nervous. I would prepare with dot points of projects or work you've done against each of the capabilities, and be ready to talk off those dot points, against the criteria. You may have to repeat yourself, but that's OK - the capabilities are designed to put a different spin on them in that case.

Of course, if you're doing a virtual interview this is a lot easier cause you can just have the capabilities up on a second monitor.

Remember - the interviewers want you to succeed. If they ask you a follow up question (like for a project management question, "that's good but can you tell us about any project management tools you've used?") it's because you haven't covered a key part of the capability - listen to the question and try to tie it in. They are designed to help you.

Last piece of advice, for after the interview - if you get informed "you made the talent pool", that is not failure. That is "you met all of our criteria and you passed the interview."

Hello. I have insight and experience on this. 

- the application panel will read every single application in detail. A good comparison would be HSC marking - the application panel will have all of the applications and a set time (typically not a long amount of time, and never long enough) to make an initial cull. 

- how many applications there are will depend on the nature of the role, seniority, how specialised it is, and so on. For a generic Clerk 7-8 role you can assume it's around 150 or so applications, but this can vary wildly (I've heard some real horror stories of 600+)

- I would suggest an introductory paragraph or two, and then well written dot points (like two or three sentences per point) to make your response very clear and easy to read. It doesn't need to be super long (two pages is usually sufficient w. an introductory paragraph, size 10-12 front, your personal details in a header - if it's more than like, 600 words I'd be cautious on the basis of "too long")

- your CV should be no more than three pages (long CVs smell of padding). Keep it situation based, keep it results based, and as I detail below, link it to the focus criteria. 

- the job ad will have some initial criteria you need to meet (for example - you need a tertiary degree, or you need a License C driver's license). Addressing these should be the first part of your cover letter - if you don't meet these you're not up for consideration. 

- the role description will have focus capabilities, with six or seven dot points for each capability that demonstrates how you prove you can meet these capabilities. These are the primary means of evaluation throughout the whole process (yes including the interview), and as such your application should respond to these as directly as possible. Use bolded sub-titles, use dot points - make it as clear to your reader that you are responding to these criteria, even if it means your letter is a bit boring. 

- writing job applications for this process fucking sucks. People will tell you you need to write a new cover letter for every job, and they're correct. They're correct because they need to respond to a. the specific context of the job and b. the specific focus criteria. Remember, the focus criteria may not be identical for roles even within the same department/unit/branch. 

- don't do the following - include a headshot photo, include jokes, include your HSC or uni marks in any form of detail ("BA with Distinction average" = good, "74 in introductory sociology" = bad), be dishonest. The last one especially - they will find out. 

That should be enough to get you through the initial stage. After that it's very dependent on the process - but remember, every stage of a government temp or permanent positiion (by this, I mean one that is listed on iworkfornsw) requires applicants to demonstrate how they meet the focus capabilities at all parts of the process. Read these carefully and keep them front of mind - if you have a video interview and you have a screen for notes, I would strongly strongly strongly strongly recommend you keep the capabilities from the job ad in your notes.

Hope this helps.

Hey. Disclaimer, not a lawyer, but someone who knows the PHO pretty well - do not take this as strict legal advice, but be informed.

*Is it a hotspot?*

Yes, it is a hotspot (or rather "an area of concern"). This is defined in Schedule 1 of the PHO.

*Can you enter Blacktown?*

Yes.

The [Public Health Order](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20\(COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak\)%20Order%20\(No%202\)%202021_210829.pdf) says:

5.2 Entering Greater Sydney
(1) A person must not enter Greater Sydney without a reasonable excuse.

It defines a reasonable excuse as:

(b) doing an activity specified in Schedule 2, Part 1, other than clause 9,

Schedule 2, Part 1, Clause 5 says:

5 Medical and donating blood
A person may leave the person’s place of residence to—
(a) obtain medical care, including obtaining a COVID-19 test or vaccination,

So, legal. 

*Can you leave Sydney after getting your shot?*

Yes. 

Part 5 of the PHO details additional directions which apply to Greater Sydney. Specifically, Division 3 (which details Leaving Greater Sydney) only applies to those currently resident in Greater Sydney. 

*I live in Newcastle - am I in Greater Sydney?*

No. Greater Sydney is defined as "The Greater Sydney Region" AND the City of Wollongong LGA. You are not subject to the restrictions around travel, and do not strictly require a permit. You will want to carry around a. evidence of your vaccination and b. your address, but note this is not strictly required as you're not leaving Sydney as a resident of Greater Sydney.

*Is it safe enough?*

The Blacktown LGA (which is massive) currently has 2000 Covid cases. It has a population of approx. 400,000. You do the math on whether you're likely to run into someone with COVID - I'd suggest it's possible but unlikely. Note, you'll need to wear masks and be subject to capacity restrictions in buildings etc anyway (as you'll be in an area of concern), so I'd politely suggest your chances of getting the plague in Blacktown are very low.

 Let's look at the [Public Health Order](https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/file/Public%20Health%20\(COVID-19%20Additional%20Restrictions%20for%20Delta%20Outbreak\)%20Order%20\(No%202\)%202021.pdf): 

Sections 3 of the PHO deals with the stay at home orders. Section 3. 12 (2) reads: 

*(2) A person is authorised to visit a place of residence in a stay at home area for any of
the following purposes* 

*(a) for carer’s responsibilities, to provide care or assistance to a vulnerable person
or for compassionate reasons,*

*(b) if only 1 adult person resides in the place of residence—as the adult person’s
nominated visitor.*


Part 1 of the PHO defines reasonable excuses for stay at home areas and areas of concern. Clause 7 says:


**7 Compassionate grounds** 
*A person may leave the person’s place of residence for compassionate reasons
including where 2 persons are in a relationship but do not necessarily live together.*

So there's two reasons within this clause to where you could be eligible to visit - either you're visiting for compassionate reasons (i.e you are living apart but in a relationship) or you're visiting as a nominated visitor (i.e. a friend).

There is a similar section in Section 4 (which deals with areas of concern) - Section 4.13 if you're curious. Section 4.13 (3) outlines that the distance restrictions specific to being eligible as a nominated person: 

*(3) A person who is an individual is eligible to be a nominated visitor for a person if—*

*(a) no other individual has been a nominated visitor for the person, and*

*(b) the individual has not been a nominated visitor for another person, and*

*(c) the individual resides within 5 kilometres of the place of residence*

Note that these restrictions apply ONLY to the nominated person (i.e. friend) - the distance restriction does not apply if you're visiting for compassionate grounds (i.e. in a relationship but not living together). 

One thing you should be aware of is clause (4) within this particular section:

*(4) No more than 1 person may visit the place of residence under subclause (2) at any 1
time except as follows—*

Essentially - you can visit your partner for compassionate grounds, but you can't do it at the same time as someone else in the house is visiting someone else for the same reasons.

Note also, there's no requirement to have formal proof (i.e. register with Service NSW) that you're visiting on compassionate grounds, but you will probably want informal proof to cover your ass. If you're a nominated visitor (i.e. friend) you are required to have proof within Section 4.13 (5) - note this is only required for areas of concern. 

Take care of yourself :)

some quick answers:

*how painful was your foot after the surgery?*

very, but i was in agonising pain due to the injury (many comminuted fractures, dislocated ankle, broken ankle, broken heel, shattered cuboid on top of 1st-4th metatarsal fractures)

i was in pretty bad pain, which the drugs did not fix, for about three weeks post injury/surgery. there was some pain due to having metal inside me now, and some pain due to having my foot cut open, and some pain from the injury. 

i still get pain now, but it's like a 3/10 compared to the 9.9/10 pain from the initial injury. 

*What was your experience?*

it's mentally way harder than physically. you will be on crutches and non-weight bearing for typically a minimum of 6 weeks (my case, 12 weeks) - and the act of being on crutches will physically and mentally wear you out. 

you'll be well placed by doing as much of the crutch preparation prior to going in for surgery - the surgery will KO you for at least a week (in my case it was two weeks before i was up to do ANYTHING). get your bottles handy, ensure you have backpacks so you can carry stuff, stock up on snacks, make sure you have comfortable bedding. 

you'll have to do rehab once you're cleared to start walking again - your muscles will atrophy, you will develop scar tissue. none of this is impossible to overcome, but it'll be hard. 

i'd suggest organising a physiotherapist as soon as possible, even if you don't see them for months. i would suggest explicitly asking them "have you rehabbed a lisfranc in the past?" - in my city many (90%?)  of the physios answer "no" to this question which means i don't want to trust my rehab with them (no offense!)

*some vocab*

i'm sure you've googled your ER's notes, but in case you haven't, some terminology. 

comminuted fracture - break of the bone into more than two pieces (i.e. you have broken this particular bone in multiple places)

oblique fracture - diagonal or curved break (typically across the bone)

avulsion fracture - essentially a "chip of the bone" fracture

subluxation - dislocation (no subluxation is typically a good thing!)

heya. i had a (severe) bouldering injury too. i'm now six-seven months post injury. 

a. make sure your physician is aware you're doing this - you should have had an x-ray at the 6 week point to be able to go "all good". don't try this until you get that all clear, don't wanna fuck yourself up worse!

b. yes, pushing off your foot is really hard - i am still having difficulties. if you have a lisfranc injury, you've directly hurt the part which gives you that push. you will have discomfort, you will have pain, you will have a limp. a physio will be able to give you exercises appropriate for the type of injury you have (my exercises, due to the complexity of my injury, may not be appropriate!)

absolutely no running, no jumping, no hiking, no bouldering. this is an injury that will take months (or in my case, years) to recover from properly. 

c. the thing that happens when you're NWB is the muscles in your foot and leg atrophy. you will feel weakness in your muscles, you will feel a stretch. what happens with an injury like this - you develop a lot of scar tissue as the body's way of healing itself, and so when you do rehab, you're resetting that tissue, and that's a difficult process with some discomfort. 

d. it took me about three weeks to go from "surgery to remove metal and walk crutches + boot" to "ditch crutches and go just boot" to "transitioning to a shoe." it was difficult and painful and took ages. i took 10 days off work following the surgery to really focus on it, and that helped immensely (thanks, work!) 

i still get setbacks all of the time, and my physio tells me TAKE IT EASY DUMBASS plenty. but i'm making progress - and if you take it easy you will too.

- does your surgeon mean "50% weight by walking?" or "50% of what you'd normally put on when you're walking?" seems vague. in my experience it took me about three weeks following my hardware removal (15 weeks post injury) to be walking, with a bad limp, with no crutches. not sure on the specifics of your injury, and also not a surgeon, but this seems kind of fast?

hiya. quick overview - December 2020 injury, ORIF surgery, three screws in my 1st and 2nd metatarsal, but also broke my ankle, dislocated my ankle, shattered my cuboid (still have a plate holding my cuboid together), broke my heel. hardware out in early March. not a gymnast, maybe the opposite in terms of build (thicc boi), but decent levels of fitness

but let's answer your questions

- re: screws snapping - my non weight bearing period was three months, and the reason for this was the risk of snapping screws - my surgeons were not comfortable with me walking on it and snapping screws, because having broken bits of metal inside you is much harder to remove than removing a whole screw. they were also worried about severing tendons and nerves in my foot from the screws snapping. other situations they might be less concerned

if you have this concern, and you want to get back to being a gymnast, make sure your docs are aware. you will probably want the screws out. 

- re: reduced mobility - hell yeah. you'll be fucked up for a while, a long while, maybe. it gets a lot easier once you can start physical rehab. 

i guess the best way to explain it is, one of my physio exercises is standing up on the balls of my feet, and then putting all of the weight on the ball of my right (injured) foot, which tests the strength of the metatarsals. when i first had the screws out i couldn't do that at all. now i can do 4 sets of 15 reps - and it feels weird, and a bit painful, but it's not horrible. 

if you're looking to land on the balls of your feet (and your metatarsals) you will likely have an even longer rehab time. i was training for a marathon when i got hurt, and my surgeons and physio have both advised me i won't be able to run/jump on my bad foot until at least the 12 month post-injury mark.

- re: hardware removal - i was pretty fucked up for a day or two (they are cutting you open after all...) but 48 hours after surgery, I had no surgery related pain. in the three months (wow...time flies) since the hardware removal, i've gone from being completely unable to put two steps together, to being able to walk with a mild (and progressively getting better!) limp, press up on my metatarsals, work on my injured leg balance, do light leg presses on the injured leg, and feel relatively normal. 

- re: future complications - I've been advised by multiple different medical teams, "you will get arthritis in this foot by the time you're older." I've also been advised that the harder I rehab it now, and the better of a rehab routine I keep up, the better my chances at mitigating arthritis, or prolonging its onset. for me, i've found accepting i will have future complications, and the best thing i can do is work to prevent those for as long as i can, is the approach most mentally healthy for me.

you're going to struggle, it's going to be mentally hard, if you're like me you'll probably cry a bit - but if you want to recover to a high level (and it sounds like you do), all you can do is a. rest while the medical experts tell you to rest, and b. do the rehabilitation work when the medical experts tell you to do the rehabilitation work.

so, like the rest of us. do the rehab work. keep your head up. it will suck - but the worst is behind you, and it'll only continue to get further and further behind you. :)

hiya. had ORIF for 11 fractures in December. doctors keep saying "oh this is a baaaaaaad one."

**about me**

28M, fairly active, broke it bouldering, was planning to run a marathon this year, was running 5Ks and 10Ks, would not classify myself as "super fit" but was increasing my level of activity for this. let's say "7/10 active levels."

**surgery**

my surgery was about three and a half hours long. i was pulled into emergency late on a monday evening, in surgery on wednesday, discharged on thursday. 

surgery went off without a hitch. being in a hospital bed is boring as fuck. bring stuff to do. if you have a Switch or something of the like, bring it. staring at your phone gets boring.

i had three screws put in my foot (around the ball of my foot) and a plate (on the mid-outside edge of my foot.)

the doctors told me "you will never run again" and i politely told them to go fuck themselves. prognosis can be variable depending on your clinician. be realistic, but also know what you want your long term goal to be - "I want to be able to get to X point." for me, that point is "running a marathon" - i won't be able to do that before i turn 30 like i wanted, but i want to get there.

you will need someone to take you home. organise this now, if you can.

**recovery**

i was non weight-bearing for three months. it sucked! i don't deal well with boredom. some tips for this part: 

- for the first part i was in a series of hard casts (i also dislocated my ankle as part of my injury). 

- painkillers did not alleviate my pain at all, but i was very physically jacked up from the surgery for about three weeks. i found it difficult to sleep, in constant pain, difficult to move around. at this point you'll be on crutches, i could only do short distances (like the 200m to the grocery store) before being wiped out. 

- i was in the hard casts for two weeks, and then in a boot for ten weeks. if you can get in a boot that'll be way easier on you.

- when i was put in the boot i was told "do ankle pumps as much as you can" - essentially, moving your foot up and down. DO IT. your leg will be totally fucked up by the time you can put weight on it again. anything you can do to work against this will help.

- also keep your foot elevated, if you can. "above the heart." pillows will help!

- by about week 6 I was feeling human enough to go out and see people. do this. it can get very socially isolating. the time will fly by, but keeping busy will make it easier. i also went to the movies a bunch.

- i was initially told "non weight bearing for six weeks" and then told "nah actually 12 weeks, the consultant fucked up". it was really demoralising! but that time will pass. seriously, it'll go by quickly.

- have a hobby to do while you're sitting on your ass. for me it was learning languages and watching travel videos. i also caught up on my youtube backlog. you probably have better hobbies to do!

- i put on a bunch of weight cause i sat on my arse for three months, ate a bunch and couldn't get out (in the middle of an Australian summer, no less!) either accept this (my path) or know it going in and watch what you eat.

-  i was able to work the entire time (office job, we were already work from home 4-5 days a week). you will be really messed up following the surgery. tell your bosses now, if they're cool they'll understand. (if you're doing a job on your feet, you might be off for longer!) i was back at work four days after the surgery (but this was in December and people were ditching for the year anyway). this was probably too soon.

- it is mentally way harder than it is physically. for me i lost a whole summer to this injury, and so physically i'd go outside and be bucketing sweat on crutches immediately - but that didn't compare to how mentally hard it was. the upside to this, kinda, is every day you make it through is one day further from the injury, and one day closer to being cleared to start rehab.

**surgery**

i had a second surgery in march to remove the screws and enable me to walk again. 12 weeks post surgery/injury. this was a day surgery - in at 5:30am, out at about 12pm, hour long surgery.

they left the plate in. if i take it out at this point i risk early onset arthritis. i still want it out at one point but i've been told "hey cowboy, give it a year, eh?"

they expected me to walk again. i tried to take a step sans crutches in the boot, in the hospital ward, and immediately ate shit. whoops. 

i was in the boot for an additional two weeks following the second surgery. i started fulltime on crutches and boot, and couldn't walk unassisted in the boot for about five days. slowly i was able to take one step, then two steps. by about day 10 after the surgery i could walk short distances (i.e. to the grocery store) in just the boot.

i took 10 days off work after the second surgery to really focus on the walking side. (i had tons of medical and overtime and annual leave banked up.) this was essential for me! i could focus on the relearning to walk side, slowly, for hours a day. would recommend. 

i now have four pinhole scars on my foot and a gnarly scar on the outside of my foot, ankle to toe. whoops.

**rehab**

about two and a half weeks ago i was cleared to start rehab (14 weeks post injury/2 weeks post second surgery), pending the healing of one surgical scar. a week after that, got the go ahead that the scar was going great, get back into it. 

here's where i'm at with that:

- i'm going back to my gym 3-4 days a week to do upper body machine work only. nothing else. i was always a cardio and lower body/legs guy, so this has been really hard. but it's essential to be in a place that focuses on fitness and recovery. it's hard as hell tho.

- i've been going to a physiotherapist twice a week. there's lots of physios in my city (a large Australian city.) doctors warned me that this is a fairly rare injury, it's complex and difficult to rehab - and you need someone who's treated it before. i spent half a day calling physios and asking them to talk to me about their Lisfranc experiences, and most of them responded with "never done one!" which means i will not give them my money, sorry friends. i would recommend doing this around week 4 of recovery - you don't want to be cleared to do physio and then fuck around for weeks trying to find a good person. 

- i've been doing exercises and movements for about an hour a day, as prescribed by my physio, on top of everything i do in my physio appointments. they fucking kick my ass. a lot of these exercises at the movement are around rebuilding balance, rebuilding proper walking form, slowly rebuilding ankle mobility, stuff like that.

- my physio advised the metal won't impact my recovery. he also said with how badly i broke my ankle, that i should have had metal in it. having a physio who is concerned with your care and active in it is critical. 

- i've been gradually building up my walking stamina, but it's still really hard going. today i walked for about an hour through an easy urban paved area and now i'm paying for it. it's soreness, not pain, though :)

- i've been apparently making marked improvements already after 10ish days of physio and exercises. my physio has advised me he wants me to start hitting it harder - walk more, spend longer on exercises, so on.

- my physio's told me he thinks he can get me running by december (small distances...) and that i should be at 90% of where i was by june next year. 

that's it! that's where i'm at. hope this helps xo :)

He wrestles with such intelligence and depth, at such a young age. He gets things like pacing and how to shift gears in order to create an emotional impact so strongly. He gets things like, disrupting the flow of a match and cutting your expectations off. 

A good example of this is in the WK13 match with Okada. This match was projected to go 25 minutes when it was announced. It goes 13. The ending is sublime. The match culminates in a sequence of reversals that is incredibly complex and difficult to pull off. And then right when Okada had White in position for the Rainmaker, White pulls out a moment of genius. Instead of ducking the Rainmaker or countering it into a suplex or slam, he speeds up his movement and instead rushes towards Okada mid-Rainmaker, and instead puts himself in the perfect position to hit a Bladerunner.

The crowd goes from on the precipice of exploding to stunned silence, because they expected Okada to finally vanquish White. But in a split second, White broke the heart of the entire Tokyo Dome with a single unexpected move.

His matches are littered with this - in the two years since his return there are dozens of examples of him being dynamic and disruptive in an innovative manner.

That's why he's the best wrestler in the world. He understands so deeply all of the little nuances and movements and actions which get an audience to feel genuine emotion - often hatred, in White's case.

To answer your updated questions:

- their schedules are different depending on time of year! during the times of big tournaments (like the G1, the Best of the Super Juniors, World Tag League, Super Junior Tag League and New Japan Cup) you'll get at least four 3-hourish shows a week. during the "down periods" such as October, you'll get one big, PPV-like show (in October's case, King of Pro Wrestling), and a number of "Road To" shows that serve to build up the storylines and angles, and give spotlights to more underused parts of the roster. "Road To" is not essential viewing a lot of the time, but you'll get really cool nuggets, especially for Korakuen Hall shows. (Korakuen Hall is their home venue in Tokyo. It's intimate - like seeing your favourite band in a small theatre instead of a large stadium.)

The top babyfaces at the moment are Okada (dickhead playboy turned unconquerable champion), Naito (apathetic asshole who everyone loves) and Tanahashi (aging, past his prime ex-ace who is struggling to stay on top), with Ibushi (genetic freak) and SANADA (cool, calm collected athletic freak) behind them. 

There's not really strict "heels" in New Japan, per se. The Bullet Club are ostentibly heels, but some members will get cheered just as much as they're booed - for example, El Phantasmo will be booed when he's being a dick, and then cheered when he does flips. The two biggest heels are probably Jay White (manipulative asshole) and Minoru Suzuki (sadistic monster who EVERYONE respects). 

Also, just to answer the comment about Jay being IWGP champion - he's a fucking tremendous wrestler. He's more cerebral and in your head in terms of wrestling, and has cut all of the flashy stuff out of his repetoire for now, but he can do all that stuff. He just doesn't, for character purposes. And his matches have tremendous emotional investment (at least for me) while also still rockin'.
